worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{2}{4-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{4-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1-{u}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\frac{x}{2})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x}{2}|<1.$
